rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clear facts benefit only people who possess and use intellect; the Qur’an and Prophet are not at fault when the Quraysh fail to learn from its reminders.
rows.anchor: People who are devoid of both knowledge and intellect can never learn a lesson from the clearest of facts.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The persecuted poor Muslims are told to fear God, unlike polytheists who make divine justice and recompense meaningless through invented intercession; piety earns a great hereafter reward.
rows.anchor: After expressing lack of hope in the attitude of the Quraysh, assurance is sounded to the poor Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that God’s earth is vast urges Muslims to endure persecution and, if worship becomes impossible in Makkah, move to a land where they can worship safely.
rows.anchor: If it is not possible for them to practice their religion in this city, then the Almighty will guide them to another land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s setting is a period when Quraysh pressure made Muslims contemplate their future in Makkah; God reassured them that another land would receive them if expelled.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this verse that this sūrah was revealed in that period of conflict between the proponents of good and evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of reward without measure assures God’s servants that patient endurance of hardship will bring a reward beyond what they can imagine.
rows.anchor: servants of God who persevere in these trials will be blessed with a reward well beyond their hope and imagination

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command that God’s earth is vast echoes the same instruction in Sūrah al-‘Ankabūt: adhere to God’s worship wherever you are.
rows.anchor: this very context in Sūrah ‘Ankabūt in the following words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the glad tidings, the Prophet is told to end accommodation of opponents and openly declare that he worships God alone with sincere obedience and is to be the first Muslim.
rows.anchor: there is no more any need to pamper his opponents; he should clearly spell out to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired directives concern both īmān and islām; a prophet must be first to accept the faith he calls others to, making Muhammad the first believer and Muslim.
rows.anchor: it is the exact requirement of a prophet’s status as a prophet that he be the first to accept the imān and islām

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must tell the Quraysh that he cannot disobey God’s directive and fears the punishment of a formidable day; he has conveyed the message and is not responsible for their faith.
rows.anchor: he cannot disobey what he has been directed to do; if he does so, then he fears the punishment of a very tough day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet declares his acquittal from opponents: he worships and obeys God alone and invites them to this, while they may worship whom they choose.
rows.anchor: This in very clear words is a declaration of acquittal and severing of ties by the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The real losers forfeit themselves and their families in the Hereafter; worldly losses are temporary, while this loss is eternal, so sacrificing the next life for brief worldly pleasure is ruinous.
rows.anchor: the real losers are the ones who have put themselves and their family in loss on the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding family to the loss makes each person responsible for seeking their family’s salvation; setting a bad example or leading them astray incurs responsibility for their ruin too.
rows.anchor: The following words of the Prophet (sws) explain this fact

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: The Prophet teaches that every person is a shepherd accountable for those under their care.
rows.anchor: The following words of the Prophet (sws) explain this fact

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ẓulal is plural of ẓullah and literally means a covering.
rows.anchor: one that covers). The verse depicts the fate of the losers mentioned in the previous verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse depicts the losers’ fate as layered fire for bedding and covering, a severe warning that they should fear God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: My punishment is something very severe; so protect yourselves from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People mistake lost worldly interests for real loss, but the true loss is permanent deprivation in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: in fact, real loss is one whose result is eternal deprivation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Acceptable worship requires sincere obedience: worship paired with disobedience to God’s directives has no weight, and obedience motivated by show or worldly interest is also rejected.
rows.anchor: the only acceptable worship to God is one which is also accompanied by His sincere obedience

rows.speaker: Sibawayah
rows.claim: Sibawayah holds that the relevant suppression is specific to a couplet.
rows.anchor: The opinion of Sibawayah that such a suppression is specific to a couplet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects Sibawayah’s restriction because the Qur’an contains several examples of this suppression; he says the word should be recited as in 109:6, given the Prophet’s pauses at verse endings.
rows.anchor: it is established that the Prophet (sws) would pause at the end of a verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṭāghūt comprehensively means anything anti-God: idols and deities, devils and jinn, or leaders who divert people from worship and obedience to God.
rows.anchor: It is a comprehensive word to denote anything that is anti-God whether idols, deities, devils and jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In contrast with the losers, those who turn from worshipping others and devote themselves sincerely to God receive glad tidings of eternal success.
rows.anchor: Here in contrast to the losers whose fate is mentioned earlier, the sincere are mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The upright listen carefully instead of responding aggressively, then follow every sound thing said to them.
rows.anchor: instead of fighting and showing aggression to the person who presents them his views, listen carefully to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their upright, truth-loving attitude makes them value the Qur’an as guidance, and God grants them that guidance.
rows.anchor: they valued the Qur’ān revealed by the Almighty as guidance to mankind and God blessed them with this guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only people of understanding benefit from God’s reminder; this restates 39:9 and parallels the reminder for people of understanding in Sūrah Ṣād.
rows.anchor: it is these people who are men of understanding and only such people can benefit from God’s reminder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verdict against Satan’s human and jinn followers is certain and unalterable, so no one can deliver its targets from Hell.
rows.anchor: this overall verdict has been given; it is absolutely certain and unalterable. Those who have become its targets will necessarily end up in Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle lākin is used here for emendation.
rows.anchor: The particle ِنِكَل here is for emendation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mabniyya means furnished rather than built; Islahi says exegetes have missed this attested Qur’anic and classical Arabic sense and promises details later.
rows.anchor: In Arabic, just as the expression بنى الدار means “to build a house”, it also means “to furnish a house”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative construction in “God’s promise” comes from an omitted verb and emphasizes the promise.
rows.anchor: The word َدْعَو ِاللّٰہ is declined in the accusative from a suppressed verb and is meant to emphasize it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Contrasting the fire-covering punishment of 39:16, the God-fearing who abstain from polytheism receive lofty, multistoried dwellings with streams beneath, a firm divine promise.
rows.anchor: In contrast to the punishment and torment mentioned earlier in verse sixteen for the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next section attacks love of transient worldly life as the reason disbelievers have hardened hearts and become averse to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: the reason which led the disbelievers to show indifference to the Qur’ān is attacked: it is their love for this transient life

none: Title and publication page only; no verse commentary.
Foreword acknowledgements, not Qur’anic verse commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 7–9 deny that favored angels intercede for rebels: the angels praise God, believe in Him, and seek forgiveness for repentant believers who follow the right path.
rows.anchor: the favoured angels of God will not intercede for those who rebel against Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 10–12 briefly show idolaters confessing their crime and pleading on Judgment Day, followed by God’s curse in response.
rows.anchor: A brief reference is given to the way in which the idolaters will confess their crime on the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 13–20 establish God’s control of mercy and calamity and exclusive right to worship and obedience; He alone masters Judgment Day, and idolaters have no intercessor.
rows.anchor: All mercies and calamities are in the control of God; hence only He is worthy of being worshipped and obeyed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destruction of earlier peoples who rejected monotheist messengers shows that their alleged deities could not help them; Quraysh are warned of the same fate.
rows.anchor: Evidence is presented from history that nations who denied their respective messengers who called them towards monotheism were visited by divine punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses–Pharaoh account warns Quraysh, encourages Muhammad and his companions to endure trials until victory, and profiles a Pharaoh’s family believer as a lesson for Quraysh and hesitant sympathizers.
rows.anchor: A specific part of the account of Moses (sws) and the Pharaoh is recounted so that a reminder can be sounded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 56–85 marshal arguments for monotheism and the Hereafter from within and around people, warn Quraysh, and firmly promise help to the Prophet and companions.
rows.anchor: The arguments in favour of monotheism and the Hereafter found within man and around him are referred to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s power and stern retribution cannot be evaded by any human technique or method.
rows.anchor: No technique or method can avail a person when He is seized by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses and Pharaoh story supports the prior claim that a people rejecting their messenger are destroyed despite worldly grandeur, and assures the Prophet and companions to persevere in their duty.
rows.anchor: when a messenger is sent to a nation and it denies him, then it is necessarily destroyed however much it may be superior

none: Qur’anic text only; this segment has no commentary.
Translation of the verses only; no commentary in this segment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ “signs” are the directives he brought to Pharaoh and his courtiers; the expression “clear authority” refers to his miraculous staff.
rows.anchor: signs) refers to the directives which Moses (sws) brought over to the Pharaoh and his courtiers
